titulo.texto: Ex Teresa Arte Actual: A Baroque Convent and Today’s Art

frase_gancho.texto: A former church of Discalced Carmelite nuns now works as a laboratory for installation, performance, and sound art.

puente_narrativo.texto: Walk a few steps along the same street to the [Palacio de la Autonomía Universitaria](cdmx_42_palacio_autonomia), at number two, which belonged to the same convent complex.

como_llegar.texto: Continue along the same street, Licenciado Primo de Verdad, a few steps away. At number eight, the [Museo Ex Teresa Arte Actual](cdmx_41_ex_teresa) awaits you, in a former Carmelite church.

guion_corto.texto: What is a work of sound art doing inside a Baroque church? That is exactly what happens here. This was the church of the convent of Santa Teresa la Antigua, home to the Discalced Carmelite nuns, built in the seventeenth century. Among its residents was Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, for a few months in sixteen sixty-seven. The architect Cristóbal de Medina Vargas designed most of the building. With the Reform Laws, the government confiscated the complex, and it served as a warehouse and barracks. Since nineteen ninety-three it has been Ex Teresa Arte Actual, a project of the National Institute of Fine Arts. It is a contemporary art space with installation, performance, and sound art.

guion_largo.texto:
A Baroque church that now houses sound art, video, and installations. That mix defines this place. You are standing before the former church of the convent of Santa Teresa la Antigua, which is now a space of the National Institute of Fine Arts. Instead of altarpieces and paintings, here you will often find installations, performances, and sound projects.

The complex was built little by little from the early seventeenth century for the Discalced Carmelites. They were a cloistered order that followed the reform of Saint Teresa of Jesus, centered on simplicity. Its original name was the Convent of San José, and the church was dedicated to Santa Teresa.

The architect Cristóbal de Medina Vargas designed most of the building and, between sixteen seventy-eight and sixteen eighty-four, gave it the Baroque style it still keeps. It is an example of New Spanish Baroque, with a nave and chapels that survive from the original structure. Before going in, look at the main portal: the double Solomonic columns of quarried stone are among its most recognizable features. The dome is later, from the mid-nineteenth century, the work of Lorenzo de la Hidalga.

Among those who passed through this convent was Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz. In sixteen sixty-seven she entered with the Discalced Carmelites and left after a few months because of health problems. Soon afterward she entered the convent of San Jerónimo, where she stayed for good.

With the Reform Laws, the government confiscated the complex in the eighteen sixties. It was a warehouse and barracks, and parts were rebuilt to nineteenth-century taste. Later it housed schools, among them the School of Dentistry, and the Rectorate of the National University. That section is now the [Palacio de la Autonomía Universitaria](cdmx_42_palacio_autonomia).

Since nineteen ninety-three, the INBA began a project here to present cutting-edge artistic work: Ex Teresa Arte Actual. It is a laboratory of Mexican and international contemporary art, focused on non-object-based practices. Among them are installation, performance, sound art, video, and multimedia. It also has a documentation center with an audiovisual and photographic collection. Its regular programming includes contemporary music concerts, film and video screenings, installations, and sound art. Non-object-based art does not aim to produce a painting or a sculpture to hang, but an experience, a process, or an action. That is why a Baroque church can become a stage.

Because the programming changes often, what you find inside will depend on the season. Check the current hours before going in. What stays constant is the contrast: a seventeenth-century church housing the most recent art. That mix sums up the Historic Center, where different eras live side by side on every block.

Very close by is the [Casa de la Primera Imprenta de América](cdmx_40_primera_imprenta). Among books, convents, and art, this block tells how the city learned to reuse its buildings without forgetting their origin.

texto.Style: New Spanish Baroque, with a 19th-century dome by Lorenzo de la Hidalga
texto.Current use: INBA space for contemporary art since 1993
texto.Key fact: Sor Juana entered with the Carmelites in 1667

texto.pregunta: Myth: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz lived her entire life as a nun in this convent.
texto.respuesta: Reality: She entered with the Discalced Carmelites in sixteen sixty-seven, left after a few months, and soon afterward entered the convent of San Jerónimo for good.
